name: Concurrency & Parallelism
description: Threads, locks, races, memory ordering, async models and the deadlocks that eat production systems.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Concurrency & Parallelism is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.answer: Concurrency is dealing with many things at once (structuring a program as tasks that can overlap); parallelism is doing many things at once (actually running them simultaneously on multiple cores).

left.title: Concurrency
points: Tasks interleave, maybe on one core
Example: a web server juggling 10,000 connections

right.title: Parallelism
points: Example: rendering video frames on 16 cores

cards.explanation: Rob Pike's summary: concurrency is about dealing with lots of things at once, parallelism is about doing lots of things at once. A concurrent program may or may not run in parallel.

resources.title: Rob Pike — Concurrency is not parallelism

cards.answer: An independent path of execution inside a program. A process can have many threads; they run concurrently and share the same memory, which makes communication easy and mistakes easy too.
cards.explanation: Each thread has its own stack and instruction pointer but shares the heap with its siblings. The operating system schedules threads onto CPU cores, switching between them many times per second.

cards.answer: A bug where the result depends on the unpredictable timing of concurrent operations — typically two threads reading and writing the same data without coordination, so updates get lost or corrupted.
cards.explanation: Classic example: two threads each run `count = count + 1`. Both read 5, both write 6, and one increment vanishes. Race conditions are hard to reproduce because they only appear with unlucky timing.

cards.answer: A mutual-exclusion object that lets only one thread at a time run a critical section of code. A thread acquires the lock before touching shared data and releases it afterwards; others wait their turn.
cards.explanation: Locks fix race conditions but cost performance when threads queue up, and they introduce new risks such as deadlock. Always release a lock on every path, including errors — language constructs like `with`, `using` or `defer` help.

cards.answer: A standstill where two or more threads each wait for a resource another one holds, so none can ever continue. Thread A holds lock 1 and wants lock 2; thread B holds lock 2 and wants lock 1.
cards.explanation: The simplest prevention is a global lock ordering: if every thread always acquires locks in the same order, the circular wait can never form.

cards.answer: Starting a slow operation (a network call, a file read) and carrying on with other work instead of blocking until it finishes; the result is handled when it arrives. `async`/`await` syntax lets such code read top-to-bottom like ordinary code.
cards.explanation: Async shines for I/O-bound work: one thread can keep thousands of requests in flight because most of the time is spent waiting. It does not make CPU-heavy computation faster — that needs parallelism.

modules.name: Models & Primitives
modules.description: What concurrency is, how it differs from parallelism, and the tools for coordinating work.

cards.answer: Concurrency is dealing with many things at once (structure); parallelism is doing many things at once (execution).

left.title: Concurrency
points: A way of structuring a program
Possible on a single core via interleaving

cards.explanation: Rob Pike's framing: concurrency is about dealing with lots of things at once, parallelism is about doing lots of things at once. A concurrent design *enables* parallelism but does not require it — Node.js is concurrent and single-threaded.

resources.title: Rob Pike — Concurrency is not parallelism

cards.answer: Processes have isolated address spaces; threads share one address space within a process.

left.title: Process
points: Crash does not take down siblings
Expensive to create; IPC needed to communicate
True parallelism even with a GIL

right.title: Thread
points: Cheap to create; own stack and registers
Communication by shared memory — needs locks
One bad thread can corrupt the whole process

cards.explanation: The trade is isolation against communication cost. Chrome uses processes per site for security; databases use threads for shared buffer pools. Green threads (goroutines, virtual threads) give thread-like ergonomics at a fraction of the cost.

cards.prompt: Why is this counter wrong under concurrency?
cards.answer: `counter += 1` is read, add, write — three steps. Two threads can read the same value and both write back the same increment, losing updates. Use a lock or an atomic type.
cards.explanation: A data race is unsynchronised access to shared mutable state where at least one access is a write. The classic fixes: a mutex, an atomic operation, a compare-and-swap loop, or removing the sharing entirely (per-thread accumulators merged at the end).

cards.answer: A mutex is binary ownership — the locker must unlock. A semaphore is a counter permitting N holders, and any thread may signal it.

left.title: Mutex
points: Mutual exclusion for a critical section

cards.explanation: Use a mutex to protect data, a semaphore to limit resource concurrency (connection pools, rate limits) or to signal between threads. Condition variables handle 'wait until a predicate holds' — always re-check the predicate in a loop, because of spurious wakeups.

cards.prompt: What four conditions must hold simultaneously for deadlock, and how do you prevent it in practice?
cards.answer: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Break any one — in practice you impose a global lock ordering to kill circular wait, or use timeouts and try-lock to break hold-and-wait.
cards.explanation: Lock ordering is the cheapest discipline: assign every lock a rank and always acquire in ascending order. Other practical rules: never call unknown code while holding a lock, keep critical sections tiny, and prefer lock-free queues or message passing where possible.

modules.name: Memory Models & Patterns
modules.description: Visibility, atomics, lock-free thinking and the async concurrency models.

cards.prompt: Why can one thread's write be invisible to another even after it completes?
cards.answer: Compilers and CPUs reorder and buffer memory operations. Without a synchronisation edge — a lock, an atomic with the right ordering, a volatile/fence — there is no guarantee another thread ever observes the write, or observes writes in program order.
cards.explanation: Memory models define these guarantees as happens-before relationships, not as caches. Sequential consistency is the intuitive model; acquire/release is the cheap one that still orders everything before a release against everything after the matching acquire.

resources.title: Preshing — Memory ordering at compile time and runtime

cards.prompt: What is compare-and-swap, and what is the ABA problem?
cards.answer: CAS atomically sets a location to a new value only if it currently equals an expected value, reporting success. ABA is when a value changes A→B→A between your read and your CAS, so the CAS succeeds even though the state was mutated meanwhile.
cards.explanation: CAS underpins lock-free stacks, queues and atomic counters, usually in a retry loop. ABA is defused with versioned pointers (a counter packed alongside), hazard pointers, or epoch-based reclamation — which is the hard part of lock-free data structures.

cards.prompt: Two threads increment two different counters and the program gets *slower* with more threads. Why?
cards.answer: False sharing: the counters sit in the same 64-byte cache line, so each write invalidates the other core's copy and the line ping-pongs between caches. Pad or align each counter to its own cache line.
cards.explanation: Cache coherence works per line, not per variable. Fixes: `alignas(64)` / `@Contended`, per-thread accumulators combined at the end, or striped counters (LongAdder). It is invisible in the code and obvious in a profiler's cache-miss counters.

cards.answer: Thread-per-request writes naturally and blocks freely but costs memory per connection; an event loop handles huge connection counts on few threads but forbids blocking.

left.title: Thread per request
points: Virtual threads remove most of the cost

right.title: Event loop
points: Callback/async colouring spreads through the code
Excellent for I/O-bound proxies and gateways

cards.explanation: The models converge: Go and Java 21 give you blocking-style code on cheap green threads with an event loop underneath. The rule that never changes is that CPU-bound work must leave the I/O thread.

cards.prompt: A payment request times out and the client retries. How do you avoid charging twice?
cards.answer: Make the operation idempotent: the client sends an idempotency key, the server records the key with the result in the same transaction, and a repeat of that key returns the stored result rather than re-executing.
cards.explanation: At-least-once delivery is what networks actually give you, so exactly-once *processing* is built from idempotency plus deduplication. The key must be persisted atomically with the effect — otherwise a crash between them reopens the window.

modules.name: Coordination & Patterns
modules.description: Condition variables, producer–consumer, read–write locks, pools, liveness failures and message passing.

cards.answer: Waiting threads can wake without the condition being true — spurious wakeups, or another consumer taking the item first after `notify_all`. Always re-check the predicate in a loop: `while (queue.empty()) cv.wait(lock);` (or use the predicate overload).
cards.explanation: A condition variable is always used with a mutex and a predicate on shared state: lock, loop while the predicate is false and wait (which atomically releases the lock), then act. Signal after changing the state, not before.

cards.prompt: Producers generate work faster than consumers can process it, and memory keeps growing. What is the fix?
cards.answer: A bounded queue between them. When it is full, producers block (or are rejected), which is backpressure: the slow stage automatically slows the fast one instead of buffering unboundedly.
cards.explanation: Unbounded queues only hide overload until memory runs out. Size the bound for acceptable latency, not just throughput, and decide deliberately between blocking, dropping and shedding load. Go channels, Java's `ArrayBlockingQueue` and Python's `queue.Queue(maxsize=...)` all provide this.

cards.answer: A mutex allows one holder at a time; a read–write lock allows many concurrent readers or one writer.
cards.explanation: RW locks help only when reads dominate and critical sections are long enough for the parallelism to matter — their bookkeeping is more expensive than a plain mutex, and writers can starve under a steady stream of readers. Measure before switching; for read-mostly data, copy-on-write or RCU can remove read locking entirely.

cards.prompt: How many threads should a pool have for CPU-bound work, and for work that mostly waits on I/O?
cards.answer: CPU-bound: about the number of cores — more only adds context switching. I/O-bound: roughly cores × (1 + wait time / compute time), or use async I/O or virtual threads so waiting costs almost nothing.
cards.explanation: Little's law (concurrency = throughput × latency) sizes pools for a target load: 200 requests/s at 50 ms each needs about 10 in flight. Separate pools for different workloads (bulkheads) stop slow I/O from starving CPU tasks.

cards.prompt: Beyond deadlock, what are livelock, starvation and priority inversion?
cards.answer: Livelock: threads keep reacting to each other and changing state but make no progress (two people stepping aside in a corridor forever). Starvation: a thread never gets the resource because others keep winning. Priority inversion: a high-priority thread waits on a lock held by a low-priority one that a medium-priority thread keeps preempting.
cards.explanation: Fixes: randomised backoff for livelock, fair locks or queues for starvation, and priority inheritance for inversion — famously the fix applied to the Mars Pathfinder lander in 1997, whose system kept resetting because of it.

cards.prompt: Shared memory with locks vs message passing (actors, CSP channels)
cards.answer: Shared memory lets threads read and write the same data under synchronisation; message passing gives each piece of state one owner and communicates by sending copies or ownership.

right.title: Message passing
points: State owned by one actor or goroutine
No shared mutable state to race on
Mailboxes can back up; ordering matters

cards.explanation: Message passing turns data races into ordering questions and scales to distributed systems naturally (Erlang/Elixir actors, Akka, Go channels). Locks are faster for fine-grained shared state within one process. Many systems combine them: actors between components, locks inside.

cards.answer: Concurrent tasks are started inside a scope that cannot exit until all of them finish; if one fails, the others are cancelled and the error propagates to the parent. No task outlives the block that created it.
cards.explanation: It fixes "fire and forget" leaks and lost errors, the same way structured programming fixed goto. Python's `asyncio.TaskGroup`, Kotlin coroutine scopes, Swift task groups, Trio nurseries and Java's `StructuredTaskScope` all implement it.

resources.title: Notes on structured concurrency, or: Go statement considered harmful

cards.answer: Pessimistic locks the resource before changing it so conflicts cannot happen; optimistic proceeds without locking and checks at commit time whether anyone else changed it (a version number or CAS), retrying on conflict.

right.title: Optimistic
points: Losers retry or report a conflict

cards.explanation: Optimistic concurrency is what `UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?` and HTTP `If-Match` ETags implement: the losing writer gets a conflict instead of silently overwriting (the lost-update problem). Choose by conflict rate — rare conflicts favour optimistic.

cards.prompt: How do you find concurrency bugs that appear once in ten thousand runs?
cards.answer: Use dynamic race detectors (Go `-race`, ThreadSanitizer), run stress tests with many iterations and random delays, and use tools that explore interleavings systematically (Java's jcstress, Rust's loom). Design to make them rare in the first place: less shared state, immutable data, message passing.
cards.explanation: A test that passes once proves little for concurrent code. Record the seed when using randomised scheduling so failures reproduce. For distributed systems, deterministic simulation testing runs the whole system on a controlled clock and scheduler.
